key_insights: Frames the Common App activities list as serving two jobs: signaling what roles/spaces a student will fill on campus, and showing they'd be an asset in those roles.

Six-step process: brainstorm every activity since 9th grade including informal hobbies and unpaid work; refine each with grade level, hours/week, weeks/year, and titles/awards; group activities into thematic clusters; prioritize which groups go first (largest group, or one tied to intended major, ranks higher; discontinued activities rank lower); prioritize individual activities within each group by recency/time commitment/achievements; then rewrite descriptions to maximize the character limits.
Suggests placing an activity that bridges two theme groups at the boundary between them so both groups appear larger and more connected.

For the write-up, recommends cramming details (titles, years, awards) into the 50-character leadership/position field and 100-character organization field rather than saving everything for the 150-character description.
Recommends dropping full sentences in favor of action-verb phrases separated by semicolons, using present tense for ongoing activities and past tense for completed ones.
Advises adding concrete numbers (dollar amounts raised, membership growth, hours) wherever character space allows, since specifics read as stronger than vague descriptions.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Common App activity fields cited: 50 characters for position/leadership description, 100 characters for organization name, 150 characters for the activity description (stated by presenter)
Example rewrite given: 'Tutor middle schoolers in STEM weekly at Thompson Community Center; selected as tutor of the month in 2024'
notable_or_distinctive: The 'bridge activity' placement trick, where one cross-category activity is deliberately positioned between two activity groups to make both groups look bigger, is a specific, non-generic tactic not commonly described elsewhere.
reliability_notes: Presenter is a paid test-prep/consulting marketer who promotes her own service at the close of the video; the character-limit and formatting advice is consistent with the known Common App format but is not attributed to any admissions-officer source.
